headline: Two Carnegie Endowment researchers argue in Foreign Affairs that China's push into AI-powered robots could decide the global AI race and that the United States risks falling behind.
score_reason: Pool 5 kept: published 12 Oct 2026 inside the window; it is an opinion essay rather than news, so no raise.
importance_line: It frames robots, not chatbots, as the next contest in the AI race, which matters to factory and logistics workers and to governments on both sides, but it is two authors' argument and forecast rather than a finding, and the claim that China is far ahead in physical AI is theirs.
summary: Foreign Affairs carries an essay by Scott Singer and Pavlo Zvenyhorodskyi of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, a policy think tank, arguing that Beijing's bet on "embodied AI", meaning AI that controls robots working in the physical world, could count for more than the United States' lead in software-based AI models. The authors, giving their own assessment rather than reporting a new event, say China backs the field as a national priority, makes about 80 percent of the world's LiDAR sensors (the laser sensors robots and self-driving cars use to map their surroundings) and could halt US assembly lines with export limits on parts, and they urge Washington to rebuild manufacturing and work with allies such as Japan and Germany.
notes: Read in full (fulltext). Opinion essay; every claim in the summary is attributed to the authors.
